topics.title: 18.1 Inlining
topics.summary: Inlining replaces a call boundary with the callee’s operations in the caller’s optimization context. It can remove call overhead and expose constants, dead branches, and redundant work. The inline keyword in C++ has important language linkage and definition rules; it is not a command forcing machine-code substitution. Inlining can increase code size and instruction-cache pressure. A small frequently used helper may benefit, while duplicating a large cold path may hurt. Let measurement and compiler diagnostics guide the decision. The best result can be a mixture of inlined hot paths and shared out-of-line slow paths.

topics.title: 18.2 Constant folding
topics.summary: Constant folding evaluates expressions whose values are known during translation. A fixed arithmetic expression can become a literal, and a condition based on a known constant can select one path before runtime. The expression must still be meaningful under the language’s rules. A compiler is not required to preserve a runtime-looking overflow merely because the programmer wrote it as a sequence of constants. Use appropriately typed constants and checked compile-time expressions when limits matter. Compile-time calculation reduces runtime work but does not remove semantic obligations.

topics.title: 18.3 Dead-code elimination
topics.summary: Dead-code elimination removes operations whose results cannot affect required observable behavior. An unused local calculation may disappear completely. A benchmark that computes a value and never uses it can therefore measure almost no intended work. Make benchmark results observable through a legitimate output or comparison outside the timed region. Do not indiscriminately mark all data volatile; that changes the workload and can block useful optimization. The goal is to preserve the operation being measured without introducing a different memory-access contract.

topics.title: 18.4 Common-subexpression elimination
topics.summary: When the compiler can prove that an expression has the same value at several points, it may compute it once and reuse the result. The proof depends on whether intervening operations can change its inputs, including memory reachable through aliases. Two identical-looking loads are not necessarily redundant if another operation can modify the location. Conversely, two differently written expressions may be equivalent after simplification. Help the compiler with clear ownership, const-correct interfaces, and limited aliasing rather than duplicating manual caches whose validity is difficult to maintain.

topics.title: 18.5 Loop unrolling
topics.summary: Unrolling repeats the loop body several times per control iteration. It can reduce branch overhead and expose independent work, but it increases code size and requires a remainder path when the element count is not a multiple of the unroll factor. A correct unrolled loop handles zero elements and the final partial group without reading past the range. Performance can worsen if extra code strains instruction storage or register allocation. Unrolling is a transformation to evaluate, not a universal improvement. Vectorization and memory bandwidth may dominate the outcome.

topics.title: 18.6 Tail-call optimization
topics.summary: A call in tail position can sometimes reuse the current function’s frame rather than creating another active frame. This can turn some recursion into constant-stack iteration. Language cleanup requirements, ABI constraints, and compiler choices determine whether the transformation is possible. A local object requiring destruction after the call can prevent a simple tail transfer. Debugging options or calling-convention differences can also matter. Do not use a recursive algorithm with unbounded depth on the assumption that a compiler will always optimize it into a loop. Establish the resource bound independently.

topics.title: 18.7 Strength reduction
topics.summary: Strength reduction replaces an operation with an equivalent cheaper sequence in the relevant context. Multiplication by a constant might become shifts and adds, or a loop might update a pointer incrementally instead of recomputing an index product. The “cheaper” operation depends on the target. Prefer clear source and inspect generated code before manually encoding a transformation whose benefit may have disappeared on the target machine.

topics.title: 18.8 Arithmetic transformations
topics.summary: Integer and floating-point transformations obey different algebraic freedoms. Unsigned arithmetic has modular identities. Options that permit reassociation or disregard special values change the numerical contract. A faster result under such options is not automatically an equivalent result for every input. Document any relaxed arithmetic assumptions, including finite-only inputs, acceptable error, and reproducibility requirements. [ R2 ]

topics.title: 18.9 Aliasing restrictions
topics.summary: Aliasing limits which memory operations can move past one another or reuse loaded values. C’s restrict qualifier is a promise about access relationships during a particular execution region, not a runtime check. Standard C++20 does not have a directly identical core-language restrict keyword, though compilers provide extensions. An incorrect non-aliasing promise can make an otherwise plausible loop undefined or miscompiled relative to the programmer’s intent. Use it only when the API actually excludes overlapping access patterns. The performance opportunity comes from a true invariant; annotations cannot manufacture that invariant.

topics.title: 18.10 Optimization barriers
topics.summary: A barrier limits particular transformations. Volatile access, compiler-specific assembly constraints, atomic operations, and external calls can impose different restrictions, but they are not interchangeable. A compiler barrier need not be a hardware memory fence, and a hardware fence needs a correct language-level interface. volatile is not a thread-synchronization mechanism. It serves specific observable-access roles, including some device interfaces under implementation rules. For concurrent application state, use atomics and synchronization primitives. For benchmarking, use a narrowly justified technique rather than disabling the optimizer across the entire workload.

topics.title: 18.11 The as-if rule
topics.summary: The as-if principle allows any implementation that preserves the program’s required observable behavior. A variable can disappear, operations can combine, and a loop can become a constant when the result is known. The preserved behavior is defined by the language and relevant options, not by the programmer’s expectation of a one-to-one translation. Undefined behavior undermines the premise on which source-level reasoning depends. Optimization is therefore a reason to be more precise about validity, not a reason to avoid optimization. A well-defined program should remain correct across optimization levels even when its instructions and timing change substantially.

topics.summary: The requirement is to compute sum(3*x[i] + 1) for a bounded unsigned sequence. The source makes the arithmetic domain explicit and returns the result so it remains observable. Optimization changes an implementation while preserving the behavior required by the language and selected compilation model. The strongest optimizations often come from proving that work is unnecessary, not from choosing a faster instruction for the same work.

SLIDE 12: 18.5 Loop unrolling

LECTURE NARRATION
Unrolling repeats the loop body several times per control iteration. It can reduce branch overhead and expose independent work, but it increases code size and requires a remainder path when the element count is not a multiple of the unroll factor. A correct unrolled loop handles zero elements and the final partial group without reading past the range. Performance can worsen if extra code strains instruction storage or register allocation. Unrolling is a transformation to evaluate, not a universal improvement. Vectorization and memory bandwidth may dominate the outcome.

SLIDE 14: 18.6 Tail-call optimization

Aliasing limits which memory operations can move past one another or reuse loaded values. SLIDE 24: 18.11 The as-if rule

LECTURE NARRATION
The as-if principle allows any implementation that preserves the program’s required observable behavior. A variable can disappear, operations can combine, and a loop can become a constant when the result is known. The preserved behavior is defined by the language and relevant options, not by the programmer’s expectation of a one-to-one translation. Undefined behavior undermines the premise on which source-level reasoning depends. Optimization is therefore a reason to be more precise about validity, not a reason to avoid optimization. A well-defined program should remain correct across optimization levels even when its instructions and timing change substantially.
